title: Week 1 derivation studio
summary: Turn the Week 1 lecture into proofs: population risk, the three lecture error sources, robust score contributions, singular OLS, ridge filtering, and classification losses.
objectives: Separate empirical risk from population risk under iid sampling
Derive the Huber score, ridge spectral filter, and logistic convexity

sourceRefs.role: ridge spectral filter and logistic setup

sections.title: Core derivation · ERM versus population risk
sections.body: ERM is the quantity we can compute from the finite sample. Population risk is the quantity we actually care about for future draws. A small training objective is not yet a claim about deployment performance.

teaching.concept: ERM is computable from the finite sample; population risk is the expected loss on future draws and is the quantity we ultimately care about.
teaching.useWhen: Use the pair to explain generalization, why validation is needed, and why a training curve alone cannot certify deployment performance.
teaching.examMove: Write both expectations explicitly and state the sampling assumption that makes their comparison meaningful.
teaching.trap: A sample average is not automatically an unbiased or relevant estimate under leakage, dependence, or distribution shift.

math.explanation: The lecture now specializes to a deterministic oracle. For a random oracle, the clarification/extension is $R_{\mathrm{pop}}(h)=\mathbb E_{x\sim\mu}\mathbb E_{y\sim p^*(\cdot\mid x)}[\ell(h(x),y)]$.
math.name: Empirical versus population risk
math.purpose: Use it to separate the computable sample objective from expected loss on future draws.

sections.title: Lecture bridge · Why iid matters
sections.body: The usual generalization story treats inputs as independent draws from the same distribution. Independence limits duplicated evidence; identical distribution makes the validation sample relevant to the population we claim to measure. Time drift, leakage, and distribution shift break this interpretation even when the split is large.

teaching.concept: IID sampling is the bridge that lets a finite sample stand in for the same population on which risk is discussed.
teaching.useWhen: Use it to diagnose leakage, duplicate evidence, time drift, or a validation set drawn from a different population.
teaching.examMove: State what is independent, what has the same distribution, and which claim fails when either condition is broken.
teaching.trap: A large split can still answer the wrong question if future data or related groups are not represented correctly.

math.explanation: The iid assumption is not a decorative symbol: it is the bridge that lets sample averages approximate an expectation under the same population.
math.name: IID sampling assumption
math.purpose: Use it to state when a sample average is intended to estimate an expectation for the same population.

sections.title: Lecture core · Three sources of error
sections.body: The slide-25 decomposition is lecture-aligned: approximation, estimation, and optimization. It is not a strict equality of scalar distances; it is a diagnostic map with distinct objects and failure modes.

teaching.concept: The lecture separates approximation, estimation, and optimization: class limitation, finite-sample movement, and imperfect search.
teaching.useWhen: Use the object transitions to diagnose a failure: oracle to best class member, best class member to sample fit, or initialization to the empirical minimizer.
teaching.examMove: Name the source and the two objects it connects; do not replace estimation with the textbook's broader generalization label.
teaching.trap: This is a diagnostic decomposition, not an invitation to merge the lecture map with the textbook's three paradigms.

math.latex: \tilde f\in\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal H}R_{\mathrm{pop}}(f),\qquad \hat f\in\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal H}\widehat R(f),\qquad f^*\to\tilde f\;(\text{approximation}),\quad \tilde f\to\hat f\;(\text{estimation}),\quad f_0\to\hat f\;(\text{optimization})
math.explanation: Approximation compares the oracle $f^*$ with the best population-risk member $\tilde f$. Estimation is the finite-sample move from $\tilde f$ to $\hat f$. Optimization is the algorithmic move from initialization $f_0$ toward the empirical minimizer $\hat f$. The lecture diagram has no $f_{\\mathrm{opt}}$.
math.name: Lecture three-source error map
math.purpose: Use it to diagnose whether a gap comes from the hypothesis class, finite data, or the optimization procedure.

sections.title: Official exercise · Huber ψ-function
sections.body: Differentiate the Huber loss instead of stopping at the phrase linear tails. Call $\psi_\delta=\rho_\delta'$ the Huber $\psi$-function or score contribution. Its per-observation contribution to the stationarity equation is bounded by $\delta$ outside the quadratic region.

teaching.concept: The derivative of Huber loss is linear near zero and capped in magnitude for extreme residuals, so one outlier cannot dominate the first-order condition indefinitely.
teaching.useWhen: Use it to derive the location-estimate stationarity equation and explain bounded per-observation contribution.
teaching.examMove: Differentiate both branches, check continuity at the threshold, then sum the score contributions.
teaching.trap: Call the derivative a score or $\psi$-function; do not claim the whole estimator is automatically robust under every design.

math.explanation: For squared loss, $\psi(r)=r$. Huber caps the first-order contribution at plus or minus $\delta$; this is a bounded score contribution, not a claim about the full statistical influence function.
math.name: Huber psi-function and stationarity
math.purpose: Use it to derive the robust first-order condition and show how an extreme residual is capped.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture recognition becomes an Exercise 1 derivation: differentiate Huber, state stationarity, and explain the bounded contribution.

sections.title: Official exercise · Singular OLS and the null space
sections.body: When the design matrix is rank deficient, the normal equation can have infinitely many parameter solutions. The pseudoinverse gives one particular solution; the null-space term changes parameters without changing the fitted training vector. This is why identical training predictions do not imply identical parameter behavior off-sample.

teaching.concept: Rank deficiency creates a family of equally good least-squares parameters because null-space directions are invisible in the fitted training vector.
teaching.useWhen: Use the pseudoinverse plus null-space term to describe non-uniqueness and to explain why off-sample behavior can differ.
teaching.examMove: Verify the null-space projection and distinguish identical fitted values from identical parameter vectors.
teaching.trap: The pseudoinverse chooses a minimum-norm representative; it does not make the original parameterization identifiable.

math.explanation: The matrix $I-\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ Phi projects onto the null space of Phi. The exact family is on lecture page 47; page 46 supplies the full-rank OLS context.

symbols.meaning: directions invisible on the training rows

math.name: Singular OLS solution family
math.purpose: Use it to describe every coefficient vector with the same fitted training values when the design is rank deficient.

sections.title: Official exercise · Ridge as a spectral filter
sections.body: Use the exercise-sheet convention $\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert w\rVert^2$. The lecture writes the more general $\lambda C(w)$ with $C(w)=\lVert w\rVert^2$, so the numerical definition of $\lambda$ can differ by a constant factor between the two conventions.

teaching.concept: Ridge shifts every eigenvalue of the normal matrix by a positive amount, shrinking weakly identified directions more strongly and restoring uniqueness.
teaching.useWhen: Use the eigenbasis to derive the shrinkage factor and explain why ridge is stable when OLS is singular or ill-conditioned.
teaching.examMove: State positive definiteness, project the normal equations onto an eigenvector, and compare with the unique OLS solution.
teaching.trap: The OLS ratio requires positive eigenvalues; ridge can be unique even when that comparison is undefined.

math.latex: A=\frac{1}{N}\Phi^\top\Phi,\quad b=\frac{1}{N}\Phi^\top y,\quad (A+\lambda I)\hat w_\lambda=b,\quad A v_j=\mu_jv_j
math.explanation: For comparison with the unique OLS solution, assume $A\succ0$, equivalently $\mu_j>0$ for every $j$. Then $\langle\hat w_\lambda,v_j\rangle/\langle\hat w_0,v_j\rangle=\mu_j/(\mu_j+\lambda)$. If $A$ is singular, OLS can be non-unique, but $A+\lambda I\succ0$ for $\lambda>0$, so ridge remains unique. The bridge is rank deficiency $\to$ non-identifiability $\to$ ridge $\to$ positive definiteness.
math.name: Ridge normal equations and spectral filter
math.purpose: Use it to derive the unique ridge solution and quantify shrinkage in each eigen-direction.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture p48 introduces regularization; Exercise 2 requires closed form plus eigen analysis. This is the distinction between lecture scope and A+ exercise depth.

sections.title: Lecture bridge · One-hot least squares to cross-entropy
sections.body: The lecturer does not regress scalar class IDs. First encode class $k_i$ as $y_i=e_{k_i}inmathbb R^K$, then compare vector scores with one-hot targets. Least-squares classification is mathematically convenient and convex, but squared Euclidean distance is not itself the classification-error measure.

math.latex: \phi(x)=(\phi_0(x),\ldots,\phi_{M-1}(x))^\top\in\mathbb R^M,\quad W\in\mathbb R^{M\times K},\quad z=W^\top\phi(x)\in\mathbb R^K,\quad \min_W\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\lVert W^\top\phi(x_i)-e_{k_i}\rVert_2^2
math.explanation: The reasoning chain is one-hot labels $	o$ vector-valued linear scores $	o$ least-squares baseline $	o$ 0–1 loss $	o$ smooth surrogate $	o$ softmax and cross-entropy.
math.name: One-hot linear classification
math.purpose: Use it to connect class encoding, vector logits, and the least-squares classification baseline.

sections.title: Lecture bridge · From 0–1 loss to a surrogate
sections.body: Classification error is the metric we ultimately care about, but 0–1 loss is flat almost everywhere and discontinuous at the decision boundary. A smooth surrogate such as cross-entropy makes score-based optimization possible while keeping the decision rule explicit.

teaching.concept: 0–1 loss is task-aligned but flat and discontinuous; a smooth surrogate supplies optimization signal while the final decision rule remains separate.
teaching.useWhen: Use the chain to explain why cross-entropy is trained even when accuracy is reported.
teaching.examMove: Name the evaluation metric, identify its optimization obstacle, then state what property the surrogate contributes.
teaching.trap: A surrogate is not the same metric as accuracy; improvement is useful only when its relationship to classification behavior is understood.

math.explanation: The arrows are a reasoning chain, not an equivalence claim. The surrogate is chosen for optimization geometry; the final classification metric remains a separate evaluation question.
math.name: Classification loss-to-surrogate chain
math.purpose: Use it to explain why a smooth training objective replaces discontinuous 0–1 error without changing the final metric.

sections.title: Official exercise · Logistic loss and convexity
sections.body: For a binary score s and label y in {-1,+1}, the logistic loss is softplus(-ys). Its second derivative is non-negative, which gives a convex one-dimensional loss in the score. The decision rule is piecewise for $s>0$ and $s<0$; the tie case $s=0$ must be resolved separately.

teaching.concept: Binary logistic loss penalizes the signed score through softplus and is convex in that score; the sign decision still needs an explicit tie rule.
teaching.useWhen: Use the second derivative to prove convexity and the signed score to derive the binary prediction rule.
teaching.examMove: Substitute the label-scaled score, differentiate twice, and handle the zero-score tie separately.
teaching.trap: Convexity in the score does not by itself prove every parameterized model is globally convex.

math.explanation: The tie at $s=0$ is a convention, not a hidden third class. The second derivative is non-negative for either label, so the score-level logistic loss is convex.
math.name: Binary logistic loss and convexity
math.purpose: Use it to derive the binary score loss, make the tie rule explicit, and verify non-negative curvature.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture introduces softmax and cross-entropy; official solutions complete the binary reduction and convexity proof.

sections.title: Week 1 synthesis map
sections.body: The complete story is a controlled sequence: define the data-generating relationship, choose a hypothesis class and loss, fit on the sample, diagnose approximation/estimation/optimization, then use rank-aware regularization when the data do not identify a stable solution.

math.explanation: The linear branch is OLS to basis functions to rank deficiency to regularization to ridge spectral filtering. The classification branch is 0–1 error to a smooth surrogate to softmax/cross-entropy.
math.name: Week 1 learning pipeline
math.purpose: Use it to reconstruct the complete path from data and modeling choices to fitted and population risk.

sections.title: Source boundary · Lecture first, exercise depth second
sections.body: The annotated lecture supplies the Week 1 scope. The official exercise sheet and its solutions are used here for derivation depth; textbook material is labeled as supporting context. These proofs deepen the lecture rather than silently changing the examinable source boundary.

examples.title: Worked derivation protocol
steps: Write the objective and name the quantity it measures.
Differentiate or state the stationarity condition before quoting a closed form.
State the rank, iid, convexity, or evaluation assumption that makes the next step valid.
Interpret the result in a direction, score-contribution, or generalization language—not only as a formula.
examples.answer: A complete Week 1 answer connects algebra to the assumption and then to the modeling consequence.

criticalQuestions.prompt: If two singular-OLS parameter vectors produce the same training predictions, what can still differ?
criticalQuestions.angle: Look outside the row space of Phi and compare coefficient norms or predictions on new inputs.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Their null-space components can differ. The training fit is unchanged, but coefficient magnitude and off-sample behavior can be very different.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does a small eigenvalue create a direction that ridge should suppress?
criticalQuestions.angle: Inspect how much the empirical design changes when the parameter moves along that eigenvector.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A small eigenvalue means the sample objective has weak curvature in that direction, so noise can cause a large OLS coefficient change. Ridge multiplies that component by $\mu/(\mu+\lambda)$.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is a low empirical risk not enough to claim a good learner?
criticalQuestions.angle: Name the expectation, the iid bridge, and the three lecture sources of error.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Empirical risk is a sample average. It informs population risk only under a relevant sampling assumption and a suitable class/optimization process; it can be low while approximation, estimation, or optimization is still poor.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What exactly is bounded in the Huber argument?
criticalQuestions.angle: Differentiate with respect to the residual and compare it with squared loss.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The derivative $\psi_delta(r)$, which is the residual's score contribution to the first-order condition, is capped at plus or minus $\delta$ outside the quadratic region.
